query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high-entropy alloys, the concurrent resistance to wear and corrosion is governed by the rapid formation and self-healing of a passivating oxide film on a nanocrystalline, high-entropy stabilized matrix that impedes crack propagation and corrosive ion penetration.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy processed to have a fine-grained (nanocrystalline) BCC solid solution with minor secondary phases (e.g., Laves phases) that promote a high density of robust grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear (via sliding abrasion) and corrosive attack (e.g., immersion in H2SO4 solution) under controlled laboratory conditions.
generation.conditions: The test environment should mimic severe operational conditions where both mechanical abrasion and chemical corrosion occur concurrently. The wear regime should be sufficiently aggressive to continually expose fresh surfaces, while the corrosive medium provides conditions for oxide reformation.
generation.structural_mediator: A passivating and self-regenerating oxide film that forms uniformly on the nanocrystalline alloy surface in synergy with the high density of grain boundaries acting as barriers to crack propagation and sites for rapid passivation.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear intermittently removes the surface layer, but the alloy’s composition and fine-grained structure enable rapid re-passivation, forming a protective oxide film. This film minimizes both wear (by lowering friction and preventing direct metal-to-metal contact) and corrosion (by acting as a chemical barrier), resulting in a synergistic reduction in overall degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a matched baseline alloy that lacks the optimized nanocrystalline structure or rapid passivation capability, the high-entropy alloy will exhibit a lower combined degradation rate, with reduced wear track depth and decreased pitting or corrosion current density under simultaneous wear-corrosion conditions.
generation.baseline: A compositionally similar alloy produced by conventional processing that leads to a coarser grain structure and less effective re-passivation dynamics under similar test conditions.
generation.boundary: The prediction applies under conditions where the mechanical wear rate does not exceed the alloy’s inherent passivation kinetics. In environments where extremely rapid abrasive loss outpaces oxide film regeneration or in corrosive environments that inhibit oxide formation, the mechanism may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in resistance remains uncertain and will depend on the interplay between wear rate, passivation kinetics, and environmental aggressiveness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of refractory high-entropy alloys processed to achieve a fine nanocrystalline structure with rapid oxide passivation capability, and a matched baseline set processed conventionally to yield a coarser microstructure with reduced passivation. Subject both sets to controlled simultaneous wear (using a sliding wear apparatus under fixed load and speed) and corrosion (immersed in 0.5 M H2SO4) conditions. Monitor degradation over time.
measurements: Wear rate and track depth via tribometer and profilometry
Corrosion current density and potential via potentiodynamic polarization
Surface oxide film and morphology characterization using SEM/EDS
Grain size and phase distribution via TEM/XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy with the refined microstructure does not show a statistically significant reduction in both wear rate and corrosion current density (or fails to exhibit the self-healing oxide film) compared to the baseline alloy under identical test conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
